title: Krishna's Rebuke of Duryodhana's Crimes
story:
For a long moment after Duryodhana finished, Krishna said nothing. The prince had just declared he would rather die on a bed of arrows than give the Pandavas a needle-point of land — and Krishna, who had come to stop a war, had his answer. When he spoke at last, his eyes were red with anger, and the sweet counsel of the morning was gone.

"You want a bed of heroes?" Krishna asked, and his quiet voice was colder than any shout. "Then you shall have it, with your counsellors. Wait only a short while — a great slaughter will follow."

Then he turned on the claim Duryodhana had just made. "You think, you of little understanding, that you have done the Pandavas no wrong? Let the assembled kings judge. Grieved at the prosperity of the high-souled Pandavas, you conspired with Suvala's son over the gambling match. How else could those virtuous, honest kinsmen of yours have been drawn into such a wicked game with the deceitful Shakuni? Gambling robs even good men of their wits; for the wicked it breeds only ruin. It was you who devised that terrible source of calamity, with your wicked counsellors, without ever consulting a man of righteous conduct."

Krishna's voice did not rise. It gathered. "Who else would have dared to insult a brother's wife as you did — to drag her into the assembly and speak to her as you spoke to Draupadi, the Pandavas' wife? She is of noble birth and blameless conduct, dearer to them than their own lives, and their queen was treated even so by you. Every Kaurava remembers the words Dussasana hurled at the Pandavas as they set out for the woods — the heartless words, fit only for the despicable, that Karna repeated, and Dussasana repeated, and you repeated."

He moved through the crimes one by one, as a man turns over stones. "You took great pains to burn the Pandavas to death with their mother at Varanavata, when they were still children — and that scheme of yours failed. Afterward they and their mother had to live hidden in the town of Ekachakra, hidden in the house of a Brahmana priest. With poison, with snakes, with cords, you sought their destruction by every means — and not one of your designs succeeded. After all that, how can you say you have not offended the high-souled Pandavas?"

Now the rebuke turned to prophecy. "You will not give them their share of their father's kingdom, though they beg for it. Give it you shall — when you lie low, stripped of your prosperity. You have done the Pandavas countless wrongs, and now you try to appear in a different garb. Your parents, Bhishma, Drona, and Vidura have begged you again and again to make peace, and you will not. Great is the good in peace, O king, for you and for Yudhishthira alike. Yet peace does not recommend itself to you. What can that be but the loss of your understanding? The deed you are about to do is sinful and shameful."

While Krishna was still speaking, Dussasana — Duryodhana's own brother — rose and turned on him. "If you will not make peace with the Pandavas willingly, king," he said, "then the Kauravas will bind you hand and foot and hand you over to Yudhishthira and his brothers. Bhishma, Drona, and your own father will give up three of us — Karna, who fights at your side, you, and me — to the Pandavas."

Duryodhana rose from his seat in a fury, breathing heavily like a great snake. He took no notice of Vidura, of his father Dhritarashtra, of Vahlika, Kripa, Somadatta, Bhishma, or Drona — or of Krishna himself. He walked out of the court, his brother and all his counsellors following, and the kings followed after them, until the assembly emptied in his wake.

Bhishma watched him go, and said to those who remained: "The enemies of a man who abandons virtue and profit to follow the impulses of his wrath rejoice to see him plunged into distress before long. This wicked son of Dhritarashtra obeys nothing but wrath and greed. I see, Krishna, that the hour of all these warriors has come."
reflection: Krishna's anger here is the anger of a witness: he lists the offences one by one — the dice, the assembly, the burning house, the poison — not to win an argument but to fix the record before the war begins. And Bhishma, who will himself fall in that war, is the one who names the hour already arrived.
next_story_tease: When the hall had emptied, Krishna turned to the elders who had let him go.
hero_scene: In the Kuru assembly, Krishna stands with eyes red in anger, one hand extended towards Duryodhana as he enumerates his crimes, while the seated kings and elders listen in frozen silence.
visual_elements: Krishna standing, eyes red with anger, addressing Duryodhana
Dussasana rising to speak against his own brother
Duryodhana rising like a great snake and leaving the court
the emptying assembly, Bhishma watching him go
